correctness.rationale: The Cayley forest-extension identity implies A_(n,k)=(n-2)_(k-1)(k+1)n^(n-k-2) trees with marked distance k. Deleting a nonmarked leaf gives P(w leaf|D=k)=(n-k-1)/(n-2) q^(n-k-2), k<=n-2. Deleting a marked endpoint leaf gives P(u leaf|D=k)=k/(k+1) q^(n-k-2), with k=1 separately handled and n=2 consistent. Summing yields µ_n(k)=(n-k+1-2/(k+1)) q^(n-k-2), q=1-1/n. Direct algebra gives µ(k+1)-µ(k)=[2(n-1)-k(k+1)^2]q^(n-k-3)/[n(k+1)(k+2)]. Its strict sign transition determines all maximizers and exact ties n=1+k(k+1)^2/2, with n=2 trivial case. Bounding adjacent cubic values gives k*~(2n)^(1/3), and uniform expansion µ(k)=e^-1[n+5/2-2/(k+1)]+O(n^-1/3) for k=O(n^(1/3)) shows maximum minus n q^(n-2)→e^-1.

originality.rationale: Best-of-knowledge PASS. The published endpoint-degree/distance regression law uses the same conditional tree path but only directly implies marked endpoint leaf probability; it does not determine other vertex leaves or the total-leaf maximizer. Full distance-profile primary paper gives asymptotic profile laws, not this finite conditional total-leaf regression. Older bivariate tree generating functions are specific residual implication risks.
residual_risks: A historical joint leaf count and two-label distance generating function might yield an equivalent conditional mean; bounded searches cannot rule it out.
The conditional improvement over the ordinary mean is only asymptotically e^-1, so the mathematical value lies in exact optimization and scale separation, not a macroscopic effect.
